book_title: Chapter 3: The Fabless Machine — Supply Chain, Working Capital & Unit Economics
question: How does Cirrus Logic manufacture, distribute, and convert every $100 of revenue into free cash flow, and where do its supply-chain and working-capital bottlenecks sit?

epigraph.quote: A fabless semiconductor company trades factory depreciation for wafer commitments and inventory timing; the art is keeping cash conversion above net income across every cycle.
epigraph.author: Semiconductor Operations Maxim

web_blocks.title: 3.1 Fabless Manufacturing Architecture: GlobalFoundries, TSMC & OSAT Partners

web_blocks.html: Cirrus Logic runs a 100% fabless model. It owns zero wafer fabs and outsources wafer production, bumping, assembly, and final test to third-party partners [1]. Wafer supply centers on two top foundries: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) and GlobalFoundries [1]. TSMC builds advanced, digital-heavy mixed-signal chips such as the 22-nanometer smart audio codecs. GlobalFoundries builds mature-node analog and mixed-signal wafers (55nm and 90nm-class) for boosted amps, haptic drivers, and power chips [1][3]. Assembly, packaging, and final test (OSAT) take place mostly in Asia via top contractors like ASE Technology and Amkor Technology [1].

Specialty mixed-signal wafers cannot shift quickly between fabs without months of re-testing. To guard supply and pricing, Cirrus Logic uses multi-year capacity deals [1][2]. In July 2021 (amended February 2025), it signed a Capacity Reservation and Wafer Supply Commitment Agreement with GlobalFoundries through calendar 2026. That deal required $195.0 million in upfront wafer prepayments, which amortized to $14.7 million at FY2026 end and $0 by September 26, 2026 [1][2][9]. It also gave temporary wafer-cost gains that helped lift Q2 FY2027 GAAP gross margin to 53.7% [2][3]. On June 30, 2026, Cirrus signed a new GlobalFoundries deal for calendar 2027 and 2028. Under it, Cirrus expects to buy at least about $600 million of wafers on a quarterly schedule, with shortfall terms [2]. This locks in U.S., European, and Singapore fab capacity outside Taiwan, cutting geopolitical risk—though it sets a binding take-or-pay floor if phone volume drops [1][2]. In short, foundry prepayments and wafer pledges act like an insurance policy. They protect autumn launch supply when capacity is tight, while adding fixed volume exposure if flagship phone shipments ever slow [1][2].

web_blocks.title: 3.2 Direct Engineering-Led Go-To-Market & Contract Manufacturer Fulfillment

web_blocks.html: Broad analog peers like Texas Instruments or Analog Devices run huge field-sales and distributor networks for tens of thousands of buyers. Cirrus Logic does the opposite. Its sales model is tight and led by engineers [1]. Teams win custom sockets directly with OEM silicon architects 18 to 36 months before launch via joint design deals and tape-outs [1][3]. Once qualified, chips ship mostly to Apple's Asian contract makers—such as Foxconn, Pegatron, and Luxshare. Direct OEM and contract-maker shipments drive the bulk of billings, while distributors serve the smaller general-market audio, smart-meter, and industrial-imaging tail [1][2]. That lean setup kept FY2026 SG&A at just $159.84 million, or 8.0% of sales. It let Cirrus put 21.7% of sales ($433.95 million) into R&D while earning a 23.0% GAAP operating margin [1]. That cost gap is a key edge against broad analog rivals. Yet it also shows why breaking into thousands of smaller PC or industrial accounts would require higher sales spend over time [1].

web_blocks.title: 3.3 Working Capital Discipline: DSO, DIO, DPO & Cash Conversion Cycle

web_blocks.html: Flagship phone launches cluster in the September and December quarters, giving working capital a sharp seasonal swing [2][3]. Inventory builds in Q1 and Q2 ahead of autumn ramps. As chips ship to contract makers in Q2 and Q3, accounts receivable jumps—rising from $220.15 million on March 28, 2026 to $365.75 million on September 26, 2026—before turning into cash in Q4 [1][2]. Full-year working-capital control improved sharply in FY2026 [1]. Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO) fell 28.1 days, from 121.3 days at FY2025 end ($299.09 million on $900.04 million COGS) to 93.2 days at FY2026 end ($240.87 million on $943.21 million COGS) [1]. Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) tightened from 41.6 to 40.2 days, while Days Payable Outstanding (DPO) rose from 25.6 to 31.2 days [1]. As a result, the Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC) shrank 35.1 days, from 137.3 days in FY2025 to 102.2 days in FY2026 [1]. Paired with $53.34 million in prepaid-wafer burn-down, that cash release drove FY2026 operating cash flow to a record $650.60 million—157% of GAAP net income [1].

web_blocks.takeaway: Full-year CCC shrank 35 days in FY2026 as inventory normalized and GlobalFoundries wafer prepayments hit zero by Q2 FY2027. That release drove record free cash flow [1][2].

web_blocks.title: 3.4 Unit Economics: Where Every $100 of FY2026 Revenue Went

web_blocks.html: Unit economics show how much of every revenue dollar survives as owner cash after factory wafers, engineering payroll, and capital spending. For a fabless chip designer, this bridge matters because high gross margins can still vanish if R&D or inventory swells. The audited FY2026 waterfall below traces each $100 of sales down to $31.87 of free cash flow, including a one-time working-capital boost [1].

web_blocks.caption: Cirrus Logic FY2026 Audited Unit Economics Waterfall (Per $100 of Revenue)
web_blocks.takeaway: Out of every $100 billed in audited FY2026, Cirrus Logic kept $52.78 in gross profit, spent $21.73 on R&D, and spent just $8.00 on SG&A. It earned $20.75 in GAAP net income. With fabless capex of only $0.70 per $100 plus working-capital release, it converted $31.87 into free cash flow [1].

web_blocks.title: Why FY2026's 31.9% FCF Margin Overstates Normalized Cash Generation
paragraphs: Disciplined analysts never project a peak working-capital release forward. In FY2026, Cirrus Logic turned 31.9% of sales into free cash flow ($636.61 million). Part of that came as inventory fell $58.22 million and prepaid GlobalFoundries wafers unwound by $53.34 million [1].

Strip out that ~$102 million working-capital boost, and steady-state FCF runs closer to $450 million–$530 million a year (~23%–26% of sales) before ~$82 million of annual stock-based compensation [1]. Even after SBC, Cirrus Logic remains a top-tier cash machine.

book_paragraphs: Whenever you and I look at a semiconductor business, the very first structural question we ask is simple: do they own the factories, or do they just own the blueprints? Cirrus Logic learned the hard way in the 1990s never to own a wafer fab again. Today it is 100 percent fabless. Its engineers in Austin, Edinburgh, and now Pavia design the intricate mixed-signal blueprints, while two giant foundry partners—TSMC and GlobalFoundries—do the physical heavy lifting of etching silicon onto wafers.

This split is deliberate and clever. TSMC builds the more advanced, digitally dense 22-nanometer smart codecs where transistor density saves battery life. GlobalFoundries handles the mature-node analog and mixed-signal wafers—boosted amplifiers, haptic drivers, and power-control chips—across fabs in the United States, Europe, and Singapore. Because you cannot simply move a sensitive analog chip from one factory to another overnight without months of re-testing, Cirrus Logic locks in multi-year wafer supply agreements. In June 2026, just as its prior 2021 GlobalFoundries contract was winding down, management signed a fresh two-year commitment covering calendar 2027 and 2028 to purchase at least $600 million of wafers. That deal buys supply security and geographic diversification away from Taiwan, though it also introduces a take-or-pay floor if smartphone demand ever stalls.

Now look at how Cirrus Logic sells its chips. Broad analog giants like Texas Instruments employ armies of field engineers and global distributors to sell tiny orders to 100,000 industrial factories. Cirrus Logic does the exact opposite. Its sales team sits shoulder-to-shoulder with a handful of flagship hardware architects two to three years before a phone or laptop launches, co-designing custom silicon. Once the chip is qualified, Cirrus ships massive volumes directly to Asian contract manufacturers like Foxconn and Pegatron. That ultra-lean commercial model keeps SG&A overhead at just 8 percent of revenue—freeing the company to pour nearly 22 percent of every sales dollar straight into engineering R&D.

book_subsections.title: Following Every $100 Through the FY2026 Cash Waterfall
paragraphs: Let's trace $100 of Cirrus Logic's audited fiscal 2026 revenue from top to bottom so you can feel the economics in your bones. Out of every $100 billed, roughly $47.22 goes to TSMC, GlobalFoundries, and Asian assembly-and-test houses for finished silicon. That leaves $52.78 in gross profit—a remarkably sturdy margin that rarely budges even in slower smartphone years.

From that $52.78, Cirrus spends $21.73 on R&D engineers and tape-outs, and just $8.00 on SG&A overhead. What remains is $23.05 in pure GAAP operating profit. Add $1.82 of interest income earned on its billion-dollar cash pile, subtract $4.12 for income taxes, and you arrive at $20.75 in GAAP net income. Now comes the fabless magic: because Cirrus Logic owns no fabs, capital expenditures in fiscal 2026 were a minuscule $0.70 per $100 of revenue—less than $14 million on a two-billion-dollar business! Add back non-cash depreciation, stock-based compensation, and a big working-capital release as inventory normalized and wafer prepayments wound down, and Cirrus Logic converted an astonishing $31.87 of every $100 into free cash flow—$636.6 million in a single year.

book_subsections.title: Reading the Working-Capital Rhythm Without Getting Fooled
paragraphs: Before we get carried away by that 31.9 percent free-cash-flow margin, let's put on our forensic skeptic hat. Working capital in a smartphone supplier breathes in a violent seasonal cycle. Every summer and early fall, Cirrus Logic builds inventory and ships heavily to contract manufacturers ahead of autumn phone launches. You can see this right on the September 2026 balance sheet: accounts receivable jumped from $220 million in March to $366 million in September as autumn shipments went out the door, temporarily pulling first-half operating cash flow down to $115 million before the winter cash harvest arrives.

More importantly, fiscal 2026 enjoyed two one-time working-capital tailwinds: management trimmed bloated inventory by $58 million (cutting inventory days from 121 days down to 93 days) and burned through $53 million of prepaid GlobalFoundries wafers, which now sit at zero. Strip away that ~$102 million working-capital windfall, and Cirrus Logic's true normalized free cash flow is closer to 23 to 26 percent of sales—still outstanding, and still far above most hardware peers, but a healthier baseline for our long-term underwriting.

book_subsections.title: Inside the $600 Million Foundry Commitment: Resilience vs. Rigidity
paragraphs: Let's pause for a moment on that June 2026 GlobalFoundries wafer supply agreement, because it reveals a lot about how modern semiconductor supply chains actually work. When you run a fabless business shipping hundreds of millions of custom chips every autumn, running out of wafers is an existential sin—your customer cannot launch a flagship phone with one missing audio codec or camera controller. During the 2021 chip shortage, Cirrus Logic wrote a $195 million prepayment check to GlobalFoundries to lock down specialty capacity through 2026. That move looked expensive in fiscal 2022 when it depressed operating cash flow to $125 million, yet by fiscal 2026 and Q2 FY27 those reserved wafers were delivering lower unit costs that pushed gross margins above 53 percent.

The new June 2026 agreement commits Cirrus Logic to purchase roughly $600 million of wafers from GlobalFoundries across calendar 2027 and 2028 on a quarterly schedule. Notice the strategic logic: GlobalFoundries operates fabs in New York, Vermont, Germany, and Singapore, giving Cirrus Logic and its flagship customer meaningful geographic insulation outside Taiwan—where TSMC fabricates the 22-nanometer smart codecs. At the same time, every take-or-pay capacity reservation carries a subtle risk: if global smartphone demand drops sharply in 2027 or 2028, Cirrus Logic must still absorb those quarterly wafer commitments or face shortfall penalties, which would temporarily swell inventory days back above 120 days. Supply-chain resilience is never free; you pay for certainty during booms by accepting modest volume rigidity during downturns.

book_callouts.title: Mentor Check: The Double-Edged Sword of 8% SG&A
book_callouts.text: Spending only 8% of revenue on SG&A makes Cirrus Logic look hyper-efficient compared to catalog analog peers spending 15%–20%. Always remember why it is so cheap: selling to one giant customer requires almost no sales force. If Cirrus ever truly diversifies into thousands of industrial and PC accounts, SG&A will have to rise.
